abstract: Inflammatory signaling and mitochondrial dysfunction are hallmarks of cellular senescence, yet how these processes are coordinated remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify I{kappa}B, a well-known inhibitor of NF-{kappa}B, as a regulatory factor that links mitochondrial homeostasis to stress-induced cell death and senescence. Knockdown (KD) of I{kappa}B did not by itself induce a fully established senescent state but instead generated a senescence-primed state characterized by cellular hypertrophy, reduced DNA synthesis, metabolic remodeling, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Time-course proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses revealed a selective reduction of mitochondrial inner membrane-associated proteins in I{kappa}B KD cells and attenuated early signaling responses to TNF stimulation, respectively. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis further indicated that a smaller fraction of I{kappa}B KD cells was predicted to transition toward a pro-apoptotic state. Among canonical I{kappa}B family members, induction of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) was specific to I{kappa}B KD, even though mitochondrial dysfunction was more pronounced in I{kappa}B{beta} and I{kappa}B{varepsilon} KD. These findings suggest that I{kappa}B influences the balance between post-stress cellular senescence and cell death through mechanisms that include maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis.
